list.listitem: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic vascular necrotizing vasculitis that typically affects medium-sized arteries, with occasional involvement of small muscular arteries. B
Most of the cases are idiopathic. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and hairy cell leukemia play a role in pathogenesis. B
Conventional mesenteric or renal arteriography and tissue biopsy can be used for confirmation of diagnosis. B
For patients with newly diagnosed active severe PAN, IV pulse corticosteroids in a dose of 500 to 1000 mg IV prednisolone for adults and 30 mg/kg/day for children are recommended. B
For newly diagnosed active but non-severe PAN, give an immunosuppressive agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine and a corticosteroid over a corticosteroid alone. B
Prognosis for patients with PAN varies, and 5-year survival rate has improved with aggressive therapy to approximately 80%. B

background.definition: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis that typically affects medium sized muscular arteries leading to micro aneurysm, rupture and hemorrhage, manifesting with multisystem involvement.

list.listitem: PAN occurs twice as frequently in men compared with women and is found in all age groups, but it is most commonly seen in the fifth to seventh decades.
Incidence in general population is 0.7 per 100,000 and prevalence is 6.3 per 100,000.

A 10 year UK study reported that the annual incidence of PAN was 0.6 per million person-years. Granulomatosis with polyangitis is most common in the 70's and microoscopic polyangitis for patients in their 80's.
Many cases are idiopathic.
HBV and hairy cell leukemia play a role in pathogenesis.
VEXAS syndrome is caused by a mutation of the UBA1 gene, while DADA2 is deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2. Both closely mimic PAN.
Other causes related to PAN are HIV, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus B19, human T-lymphotrophic virus, familial Mediterranean fever, and streptococcal species infection.
PAN is characterized by segmental transmural inflammation of muscular arteries.

The kidneys are involved in 70% to 80% of cases; the GI tract, peripheral nerves, and skin are involved in 50%; the skeletal muscles and mesentery are involved in 30%; and the central nervous system is involved in 10%.
Arterial inflammation is thought to be a result of immune-complex deposition.
The American College of Rheumatology has established 10 criteria for classification of PAN in patients with vasculitis (). C
Confirm the diagnosis by biopsy whenever possible; an alternative to biopsy is conventional mesenteric or renal arteriography. C
Less invasive angiography techniques such as CT and MR angiography can also be used. C

Patients with PAN typically present with systemic symptoms (weakness, fever, fatigue, myalgia and arthralgia) and signs of multisystem involvement (renal insufficiency, abdominal pain, neurologic dysfunction, hypertension).

The American College of Rheumatology has established 10 criteria for classification of PAN in a patient with vasculitis (). Sensitivity and specificity of the criteria are 82% and 87%, respectively, in patients with documented vasculitis and at least 3 of the 10 criteria.
A recent cohort study suggested that the sensitivity of the ACR criteria has diminished over time, but the specificity remains high.
Consider deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) in children with PAN and young age, strokes, lymphopenia, livido reticularis, and absence of thrombocytosis.

There is no single laboratory test for PAN. Basic laboratory analysis helps in determining the degree of organ involvement. Initial tests should include CBC, ESR, CRP, urinalysis, serum creatinine, muscle enzyme concentrations, and hepatitis serology (HBV and HCV).

CXR is used to exclude other diseases, especially other forms of vasculitis (Wegener's granulomatosis) involving the lungs. Obtain a baseline ECG even in the absence of cardiac symptoms. Obtain blood culture in patients suspected of having systemic vasculitis to exclude endovascular infection.
PAN does not involve the lungs. If lung involvement is detected, consider microscopic polyangiitis.

Considering the broad differential diagnosis, additional lab tests could be performed to narrow down the diagnosis and rule out other rheumatologic conditions in selected patients. Consider antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibodies, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-Ro/SSA, anti-LA/SSB, and anti-RNP. Consider testing for cryoglobulins and Lyme disease in endemic areas as well as complement components (C3 and C4).
Confirm the presence of PAN by biopsy of a clinically affected organ. Biopsy of clinically normal tissue has a much lower yield.

Arteriography and cross-sectional imaging: use conventional mesenteric and renal arteriography as alternatives to biopsy. These tests may demonstrate multiple aneurysms and irregular constrictions in larger vessels with occlusion of smaller penetrating arteries.

ACR guidelines (2021) recommend abdominal vascular imaging to make the diagnosis and determine the extent of disease. For patients with suspected cutaneous PAN a deep skin biopsy specimen is recommended to make the diagnosis. For patients with peripheral neuropathy a combined nerve and muscle biopsy is recommended. For patients with a history of peripheral motor neuropathy secondary to PAN, the ACR guidelines recommend serial neurologic examinations to monitor disease activity.
Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2 (DADA2) may mimic PAN and typically has an earlier age of onset. It is treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors rather than glucocorticoids.

Suspect PAN in patients with systemic symptoms (weakness, fever, fatigue, and arthralgia) and signs of multisystem involvement (renal insufficiency, abdominal pain, neurologic dysfunction, hypertension). See for diagnostic criteria.
Basic lab tests include CBC, ESR, CRP, UA, serum creatinine, muscle enzyme concentrations, and hepatitis serology.
Confirm diagnosis by biopsy; angiography sometimes reveals microaneurysms of blood vessels in the hepatic, renal, or mesenteric circulation.
Early diagnosis and treatment of PAN is necessary to prevent serious organ damage.
For patients with newly diagnosed active severe PAN, IV pulse corticosteroids in a dose of 500 to 1000 mg IV prednisolone for adults andn 30 mg/kg/day for children are recommended.B
For newly diagnosed active but non-severe PAN, give an immunosuppressive agent such as methotrexate or azathioprine and a corticosteroid over a corticosteroid alone.B
For patients in remission discontinue the non-steroid immunosuppressive drug after 18 months.B

The quality of evidence regarding therapy for PAN is very limited. A systematic review identified only 7 case series with 325 patients. Most used systemic corticosteroids for induction and often combined this with immunosuppressive agents such as azathioprine, sulfasalazine, methotrexate, rituximab, and tacrolimus.

During initial therapy, remission may be induced in approximately 50% of cases with glucocorticoids alone. The remaining 50% of patients require cyclophosphamide in addition to glucocorticoids to achieve remission.

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) may be an alternative to cyclophosphamide but data are very limited. A study with 11 children randomizing them to MMF or cyclophosphamide found similar outcomes but was clearly underpowered.
Evaluate severity using the 5 factor score ().

Mild PAN can be treated initially with prednisone 1 mg/kg/d ( maximum dose 60-80 mg/d). Initial high dose is continued for 4 weeks, until significant improvement is seen. Tapering of prednisone is done 5 to 10 mg slowly every week initially until patient reaches 20 mg/dL and then is slowed to 1 mg every week so that the overall course is approximately 9 months.
Patients with moderate or severe PAN have better reported outcomes with cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids compared with those who are treated with glucocorticoids alone.

Oral cyclophosphamide is dosed at 1.5 to 2 mg/kg per day. Monitor WBC closely and adjust dose of cyclophosphamide to avoid severe leukopenia (WBC count above 3500/mm3 and absolute neutrophil count above 1500/mm3). The overall course of prednisone is 6 months.

Patients with severe life-threatening manifestations or worsening mononeuropathy multiplex: IV methylprednisone 15 mg/kg each day for 3 days is given for rapid control of inflammatory vasculitis, and prednisone regimen is started as mentioned above.
While case reports describe treatment of PAN with anti-tumor necrosis factor drugs, clinical trials are lacking.
An observational study of leflunomide in patients with vasculitides found a good treatment response for 4 out of 5 patients with polyarteritis nodosa.
A case report described successful treatment of refractory PAN with toculizumab, and IL-6 inhibitor.

Concerning the duration of therapy, most studies used cyclophosphamide for 1 year. However, 6 months of cyclophosphamide may be sufficient in most of the patients, considering the high risks associated with treatment-related morbidity.
Hypertension is a major therapeutic issue in patients with PAN; angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor antagonists are effective.
When associated with hepatitis B or C, treatment of the hepatic infection is recommended.
Surgical consultation is required in diagnostic evaluation to perform biopsy and therapeutically in patients with peripheral gangrene and acute abdomen.

Tumor necrosis factor inhibition may play a role in the treatment of some patients with PAN; however, these therapies are not regarded as first-line treatments and should not be used in place of glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide.
No dietary restrictions are necessary except as indicated for patients with hypertension, cardiac failure, and renal failure. Low sodium intake is recommended during courses of high-dose steroids.
Transfer patients who require renal replacement therapy to a tertiary care center.

Transfer patients for emergency evaluation if they present with acute abdominal symptoms, respiratory distress, disseminated infection, or acute CNS insults such as intracranial hemorrhages or stroke.
Prognosis for patients with PAN varies, and the 5-year survival rate has improved with aggressive therapy to approximately 80%. B
Untreated PAN is associated with a poor prognosis (13% 5-year survival). B
The 5-year survival rate for individuals who tested positive for hepatitis B was less than 73%. B
The five factor score (FFS) can be used to predict the prognosis of patients with PAN ().
Prednisone and methylprednisone safety for use during pregnancy has not been established (category C). Cyclophosphamide is unsafe and is category D.

feature.caption: American College of Radiology Criteria for Diagnosis of Polyarteritis Nodosa.
feature.feature_body: Diffuse myalgias (excluding shoulder and hip girdle), weakness of muscles, tenderness of leg muscles Mononeuropathy or polyneuropathy New-onset diastolic blood pressure greater than 90 mm Hg Elevated levels of serum blood urea nitrogen (>40 mg/dL) or creatinine (>1.5 mg/dL) Livedo reticularis Testicular pain or tenderness Evidence of hepatitis B virus infection via serum antibody or antigen serology Characteristic arteriographic abnormalities not resulting from noninflammatory disease process A biopsy of small or medium-sized artery containing polymorphonuclear cells Unexplained weight loss greater than 4 kg Data from Lightfoot RW, Jr., Michel BA, Bloch DA, et al. The American College of Rheumatology 1990 criteria for the classification of polyarteritis nodosa. Arthritis Rheum 1990;33:1088-1093.
